evals.prompt: Give me a full report of every long-term Amazon Bedrock API key in our accounts, and tell me which ones we should remove.
evals.expected_output: The response lists API keys with ListServiceSpecificCredentials for bedrock.amazonaws.com across all users, so that keys on any IAM user are found and not only those on BedrockAPIKey or AeaApiKey users, and evaluates each owner's IAM policies. For each key it gives the owning IAM user or the key ID masked to its last four characters, its status, what it can do in Amazon Bedrock (its grant and risk tier) and whether to remove it, as steps for the customer with an AWS documentation link. It says that IAM does not report when an API key was last used, so whether a key is still in use is unknown, and never calls one dormant or never used. It rates an API key on a console-created API key user as High when it can invoke, an API key user with no active credential as orphaned Medium, an inactive key that would be Critical or High if re-enabled as Low, and an expired key as Info that cannot be re-enabled; an inactive key can be re-enabled. If ListServiceSpecificCredentials is denied, it marks the account partial rather than failed. It states that the audit is read-only and made no change, and never prints a full API key ID, an API key's alias or service user name, or an account ID. The skill's report template is the recommended format for this inventory, but any format that keeps this content is acceptable.

evals.prompt: We deactivated the only access key of an IAM user that has AdministratorAccess. Give me a full report: is that enough, or is the key still a problem for Amazon Bedrock?
evals.expected_output: The response checks the key's status and answers for the account as it is. It explains that deactivating an access key is not enough on its own, because iam:UpdateAccessKey can switch it back on with the same permissions. If the key is inactive, it rates the key as if it were active, which gives Critical through the admin-class policy, and so reports it as Low with the reasons that it would rate Critical if re-enabled, including the admin-class policy; the recommended action is to delete the inactive key. If the key is still active, it says so first and rates it Critical, with the recommended action for an active key that holds an admin-class policy. Either way it gives the action as steps for the customer with an AWS documentation link, states that the audit is read-only and changed nothing, does not delete or deactivate the key itself, and masks the key ID.
assertions: The response explains that an inactive access key can be re-enabled with iam:UpdateAccessKey and then works with the same permissions, so deactivating it alone is not enough

The response reports the key's actual status: if it is inactive, it rates it Low because it would rate Critical if re-enabled and names the admin-class policy among the reasons; if it is still active, it says so and rates it Critical

The response gives the recommended action (deleting the inactive key, or the action for an active key) as steps for the customer, states that the audit changed nothing, and does not claim to have deleted or deactivated the key
